How Bra Sizes Are Determined: Measurements, Cup Progression and Fit

Learn how underbust and bust measurements are used to produce a starting bra size, why cup progressions differ, and why fit checks still matter.

Measurement-Based Sizing

A bra size combines a band label with a cup label. A measurement calculator can provide a useful starting point, but it cannot determine garment fit by numbers alone. ISO 8559-1:2017 standardizes definitions for clothing anthropometric measurements; it does not establish one universal bra-size formula.

Band Starting Point

Measure the underbust according to the instructions for the sizing system being used, then apply that system's band convention. Avoid presenting a single rounding rule as universal because commercial size charts differ.

Cup Starting Point

A simple method is to compare the full-bust and underbust measurements. This site uses approximately one cup step per inch of difference for its basic calculator. That is a starting convention, not a universal industry standard.

Why Fit Checking Matters

Research comparing tape-measure sizing with professional fit criteria found significant differences between the two approaches. The researchers recommended putting more emphasis on fit criteria and less on treating a calculated size as absolute. citeturn1search0

Frequently Asked Questions

Answers about sizing methods, measurements, and fit considerations.

What does the number in a bra size represent? ▾

It is a band label associated with the ribcage measurement under a particular sizing convention. It should not be treated as a universal direct measurement in every market.

What does the cup letter represent? ▾

It represents a cup category within a particular sizing system. Measurement-difference methods use the relationship between bust and underbust as a starting point, but commercial fit also depends on garment construction.

Sources & Standards

  • ISO 8559-1:2017, Size designation of clothes — Part 1: Anthropometric definitions for body measurement
  • White & Scurr (2012), Ergonomics, DOI 10.1080/00140139.2011.647096
